Case Study: Tourism New Zealand website
New Zealand is a small country of four million inhabitants, a long-haul flight from all the
major tourist-generating markets of the world. Tourism currently makes up 9% of the
country’s gross domestic product, and is the country’s largest export sector. Unlike other
export sectors, which make products and then sell them overseas, tourism brings its
customers to New Zealand. The product is the country itself – the people, the places and
the experiences. In 1999, Tourism New Zealand launched a campaign to communicate
a new brand position to the world. The campaign focused on New Zealand’s scenic
beauty, exhilarating outdoor activities and authentic Maori culture, and it made New
Zealand one of the strongest national brands in the world.
A key feature of the campaign was the website www.newzealand.com, which provided
potential visitors to New Zealand with a single gateway to everything the destination had
to offer. The heart of the website was a database of tourism services operators, both
those based in New Zealand and those based abroad which offered tourism services to
the country. Any tourism-related business could be listed by filling in a simple form. This
meant that even the smallest bed and breakfast address or specialist activity provider
could gain a web presence with access to an audience of long-haul visitors. In addition,
because participating businesses were able to update the details they gave on a
regular basis, the information provided remained accurate. And to maintain and improve
standards, Tourism New Zealand organised a scheme whereby organisations appearing
on the website underwent an independent evaluation against a set of agreed national
standards of quality. As part of this, the effect of each business on the environment was
considered.
To communicate the New Zealand experience, the site also carried features relating
to famous people and places. One of the most popular was an interview with former
New Zealand All Blacks rugby captain Tana Umaga. Another feature that attracted a
lot of attention was an interactive journey through a number of the locations chosen
for blockbuster films which had made use of New Zealand’s stunning scenery as a
backdrop. As the site developed, additional features were added to help independent
travellers devise their own customised itineraries. To make it easier to plan motoring
holidays, the site catalogued the most popular driving routes in the country, highlighting
different routes according to the season and indicating distances and times.

Reading
Later, a Travel Planner feature was added, which allowed visitors to click and ‘bookmark’
places or attractions they were interested in, and then view the results on a map. The
Travel Planner offered suggested routes and public transport options between the
chosen locations. There were also links to accommodation in the area. By registering
with the website, users could save their Travel Plan and return to it later, or print it out
to take on the visit. The website also had a ‘Your Words’ section where anyone could
submit a blog of their New Zealand travels for possible inclusion on the website.
The Tourism New Zealand website won two Webby awards for online achievement
and innovation. More importantly perhaps, the growth of tourism to New Zealand was
impressive. Overall tourism expenditure increased by an average of 6.9% per year
between 1999 and 2004. From Britain, visits to New Zealand grew at an average annual
rate of 13% between 2002 and 2006, compared to a rate of 4% overall for British
visits abroad.
The website was set up to allow both individuals and travel organisations to create
itineraries and travel packages to suit their own needs and interests. On the website,
visitors can search for activities not solely by geographical location, but also by the
particular nature of the activity. This is important as research shows that activities are the
key driver of visitor satisfaction, contributing 74% to visitor satisfaction, while transport
and accommodation account for the remaining 26%. The more activities that visitors
undertake, the more satisfied they will be. It has also been found that visitors enjoy
cultural activities most when they are interactive, such as visiting a marae (meeting
ground) to learn about traditional Maori life. Many long-haul travellers enjoy such
learning experiences, which provide them with stories to take home to their friends and
family. In addition, it appears that visitors to New Zealand don’t want to be ‘one of the
crowd’ and find activities that involve only a few people more special and meaningful.
It could be argued that New Zealand is not a typical destination. New Zealand is a small
country with a visitor economy composed mainly of small businesses. It is generally
perceived as a safe English-speaking country with a reliable transport infrastructure.
Because of the long-haul flight, most visitors stay for longer (average 20 days) and want
to see as much of the country as possible on what is often seen as a once-in-a-lifetime
visit. However, the underlying lessons apply anywhere – the effectiveness of a strong
brand, a strategy based on unique experiences and a comprehensive and user-friendly
website.

Why being bored is stimulating – and useful, too
This most common of emotions is turning out to be more interesting than
we thought
A
We all know how it feels – it’s impossible to keep your mind on anything, time
stretches out, and all the things you could do seem equally unlikely to make you
feel better. But defining boredom so that it can be studied in the lab has proved
difficult. For a start, it can include a lot of other mental states, such as frustration,
apathy, depression and indifference. There isn’t even agreement over whether
boredom is always a low-energy, flat kind of emotion or whether feeling agitated
and restless counts as boredom, too. In his book, Boredom: A Lively History, Peter
Toohey at the University of Calgary, Canada, compares it to disgust – an emotion
that motivates us to stay away from certain situations. ‘If disgust protects humans
from infection, boredom may protect them from “infectious” social situations,’
he suggests.
B
By asking people about their experiences of boredom, Thomas Goetz and his team
at the University of Konstanz in Germany have recently identified five distinct types:
indifferent, calibrating, searching, reactant and apathetic. These can be plotted on
two axes – one running left to right, which measures low to high arousal, and the
other from top to bottom, which measures how positive or negative the feeling is.
Intriguingly, Goetz has found that while people experience all kinds of boredom,
they tend to specialise in one. Of the five types, the most damaging is ‘reactant’
boredom with its explosive combination of high arousal and negative emotion. The
most useful is what Goetz calls ‘indifferent’ boredom: someone isn’t engaged in
anything satisfying but still feels relaxed and calm. However, it remains to be seen
whether there are any character traits that predict the kind of boredom each of us
might be prone to.
C
Psychologist Sandi Mann at the University of Central Lancashire, UK, goes further.
‘All emotions are there for a reason, including boredom,’ she says. Mann has found
that being bored makes us more creative. ‘We’re all afraid of being bored but in
actual fact it can lead to all kinds of amazing things,’ she says. In experiments
published last year, Mann found that people who had been made to feel bored by
copying numbers out of the phone book for 15 minutes came up with more creative
ideas about how to use a polystyrene cup than a control group. Mann concluded
that a passive, boring activity is best for creativity because it allows the mind
to wander. In fact, she goes so far as to suggest that we should seek out more
boredom in our lives.
D
Psychologist John Eastwood at York University in Toronto, Canada, isn’t convinced.
‘If you are in a state of mind-wandering you are not bored,’ he says. ‘In my view,
by definition boredom is an undesirable state.’ That doesn’t necessarily mean
that it isn’t adaptive, he adds. ‘Pain is adaptive – if we didn’t have physical pain,
bad things would happen to us. Does that mean that we should actively cause
pain? No. But even if boredom has evolved to help us survive, it can still be toxic

if allowed to fester.’ For Eastwood, the central feature of boredom is a failure to
put our ‘attention system’ into gear. This causes an inability to focus on anything,
which makes time seem to go painfully slowly. What’s more, your efforts to improve
the situation can end up making you feel worse. ‘People try to connect with the
world and if they are not successful there’s that frustration and irritability,’ he says.
Perhaps most worryingly, says Eastwood, repeatedly failing to engage attention
can lead to a state where we don’t know what to do any more, and no longer care.
E
Eastwood’s team is now trying to explore why the attention system fails. It’s early
days but they think that at least some of it comes down to personality. Boredom
proneness has been linked with a variety of traits. People who are motivated by
pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly. Other personality traits, such as curiosity,
are associated with a high boredom threshold. More evidence that boredom has
detrimental effects comes from studies of people who are more or less prone to
boredom. It seems those who bore easily face poorer prospects in education,
their career and even life in general. But of course, boredom itself cannot kill —
it’s the things we do to deal with it that may put us in danger. What can we do to
alleviate it before it comes to that? Goetz’s group has one suggestion. Working with
teenagers, they found that those who ‘approach’ a boring situation – in other words,
see that it’s boring and get stuck in anyway – report less boredom than those who
try to avoid it by using snacks, TV or social media for distraction.
F
Psychologist Francoise Wemelsfelder speculates that our over-connected lifestyles
might even be a new source of boredom. ‘In modern human society there is a lot of
overstimulation but still a lot of problems finding meaning,’ she says. So instead of
seeking yet more mental stimulation, perhaps we should leave our phones alone,
and use boredom to motivate us to engage with the world in a more
meaningful way.

Artificial artists
Can computers really create works of art?
The Painting Fool is one of a growing number of computer programs which, so their
makers claim, possess creative talents. Classical music by an artificial composer has
had audiences enraptured, and even tricked them into believing a human was behind
the score. Artworks painted by a robot have sold for thousands of dollars and been hung
in prestigious galleries. And software has been built which creates art that could not
have been imagined by the programmer.
Human beings are the only species to perform sophisticated creative acts regularly.
If we can break this process down into computer code, where does that leave human
creativity? ‘This is a question at the very core of humanity,’ says Geraint Wiggins, a
computational creativity researcher at Goldsmiths, University of London. ‘It scares a lot
of people. They are worried that it is taking something special away from what it means
to be human.’
To some extent, we are all familiar with computerised art. The question is: where does
the work of the artist stop and the creativity of the computer begin? Consider one of the
oldest machine artists, Aaron, a robot that has had paintings exhibited in London’s Tate
Modern and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Aaron can pick up a paintbrush
and paint on canvas on its own. Impressive perhaps, but it is still little more than a tool to
realise the programmer’s own creative ideas.
Simon Colton, the designer of the Painting Fool, is keen to make sure his creation
doesn’t attract the same criticism. Unlike earlier ‘artists’ such as Aaron, the Painting Fool
only needs minimal direction and can come up with its own concepts by going online for
material. The software runs its own web searches and trawls through social media sites.
It is now beginning to display a kind of imagination too, creating pictures from scratch.
One of its original works is a series of fuzzy landscapes, depicting trees and sky. While
some might say they have a mechanical look, Colton argues that such reactions arise
from people’s double standards towards software-produced and human-produced
art. After all, he says, consider that the Painting Fool painted the landscapes without
referring to a photo. ‘If a child painted a new scene from its head, you’d say it has a
certain level of imagination,’ he points out. ‘The same should be true of a machine.’
Software bugs can also lead to unexpected results. Some of the Painting Fool’s
paintings of a chair came out in black and white, thanks to a technical glitch. This gives
the work an eerie, ghostlike quality. Human artists like the renowned Ellsworth Kelly are
lauded for limiting their colour palette – so why should computers be any different?
24

Reading
Researchers like Colton don’t believe it is right to measure machine creativity directly
to that of humans who ‘have had millennia to develop our skills’. Others, though, are
fascinated by the prospect that a computer might create something as original and
subtle as our best artists. So far, only one has come close. Composer David Cope
invented a program called Experiments in Musical Intelligence, or EMI. Not only did
EMI create compositions in Cope’s style, but also that of the most revered classical
composers, including Bach, Chopin and Mozart. Audiences were moved to tears, and
EMI even fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach.
Not everyone was impressed however. Some, such as Wiggins, have blasted Cope’s
work as pseudoscience, and condemned him for his deliberately vague explanation of
how the software worked. Meanwhile, Douglas Hofstadter of Indiana University said
EMI created replicas which still rely completely on the original artist’s creative impulses.
When audiences found out the truth they were often outraged with Cope, and one music
lover even tried to punch him. Amid such controversy, Cope destroyed EMI’s
vital databases.
But why did so many people love the music, yet recoil when they discovered how it
was composed? A study by computer scientist David Moffat of Glasgow Caledonian
University provides a clue. He asked both expert musicians and non-experts to assess
six compositions. The participants weren’t told beforehand whether the tunes were
composed by humans or computers, but were asked to guess, and then rate how much
they liked each one. People who thought the composer was a computer tended to dislike
the piece more than those who believed it was human. This was true even among the
experts, who might have been expected to be more objective in their analyses.
Where does this prejudice come from? Paul Bloom of Yale University has a suggestion:
he reckons part of the pleasure we get from art stems from the creative process behind
the work. This can give it an ‘irresistible essence’, says Bloom. Meanwhile, experiments
by Justin Kruger of New York University have shown that people’s enjoyment of an
artwork increases if they think more time and effort was needed to create it. Similarly,
Colton thinks that when people experience art, they wonder what the artist might have
been thinking or what the artist is trying to tell them. It seems obvious, therefore, that
with computers producing art, this speculation is cut short – there’s nothing to explore.
But as technology becomes increasingly complex, finding those greater depths in
computer art could become possible. This is precisely why Colton asks the Painting
Fool to tap into online social networks for its inspiration: hopefully this way it will choose
themes that will already be meaningful to us.

sentences.structure: This 回指低门槛登记；that 宾语从句中，bed and breakfast address 与 specialist activity provider 是由 or 连接的两个并列中心，even 突出规模最小的登记地址或服务商也能受益；with access to... 补充这种线上存在带来的实际价值。

vocabulary.meaning: 住宿加早餐旅店的地址或登记项；保留原文 address 的信息
获得线上曝光和可见度

sentences.text: In addition, because participating businesses were able to update the details they gave on a regular basis, the information provided remained accurate.
sentences.translation: 此外，由于参与企业能够定期更新自己提供的详细信息，网站上的信息得以保持准确。
sentences.structure: because 原因从句解释信息为何可靠；they gave 是省略关系代词的定语从句，provided 是过去分词后置修饰 information。

sentences.text: And to maintain and improve standards, Tourism New Zealand organised a scheme whereby organisations appearing on the website underwent an independent evaluation against a set of agreed national standards of quality.
sentences.translation: 为了维持并提高标准，新西兰旅游局还组织了一套机制：网站上的机构须依据一套共同认可的全国质量标准接受独立评估。
sentences.structure: 句首不定式表目的；whereby 引导定语从句说明 scheme 的运作方式；appearing... 修饰 organisations，underwent 是正式语体中的“经历、接受”。

vocabulary.meaning: 机构；组织；本句复数指网站上接受评估的机构
依据一套标准进行衡量
共同认可的全国质量标准

sentences.text: As part of this, the effect of each business on the environment was considered.
sentences.translation: 作为该评估的一部分，每家企业对环境的影响也会被纳入考量。
sentences.structure: 被动语态 was considered 隐去评估者，突出评估内容；on the environment 限定 effect 的作用对象。

sentences.text: To communicate the New Zealand experience, the site also carried features relating to famous people and places.
sentences.translation: 为了传达新西兰体验，该网站还刊载了与名人和著名地点有关的专题内容。
sentences.structure: 不定式置前表目的；主干 the site carried features 中 carry 不是“携带”，而是媒体语境的“刊载”。

sentences.text: Another feature that attracted a lot of attention was an interactive journey through a number of the locations chosen for blockbuster films which had made use of New Zealand’s stunning scenery as a backdrop.

vocabulary.meaning: 专题内容；本句指互动式地点游览专题

sentences.text: As the site developed, additional features were added to help independent travellers devise their own customised itineraries.
sentences.translation: 随着网站发展，又增添了更多功能，帮助自由行游客设计自己的个性化行程。

sentences.text: To make it easier to plan motoring holidays, the site catalogued the most popular driving routes in the country, highlighting different routes according to the season and indicating distances and times.
sentences.translation: 为方便游客规划自驾假期，网站把全国最受欢迎的驾车路线编成目录，并按季节突出不同路线，同时标明距离与所需时间。
sentences.structure: To make it easier... 表目的，it 是形式宾语；主干 the site catalogued...，两个现在分词 highlighting 与 indicating 并列说明目录提供的信息。

sentences.text: Later, a Travel Planner feature was added, which allowed visitors to click and ‘bookmark’ places or attractions they were interested in, and then view the results on a map.
sentences.translation: 后来，网站新增了“旅行规划器”功能，游客可以点击并“收藏”感兴趣的地点或景点，然后在地图上查看结果。
sentences.structure: 主句用被动引入新功能；which 从句解释用途，allowed visitors to... 后并列 click/bookmark 与 view；they were interested in 修饰 places or attractions。

vocabulary.meaning: 功能；本句指旅行规划器功能

sentences.text: The Travel Planner offered suggested routes and public transport options between the chosen locations.

sentences.structure: 简单主谓宾结构；suggested 与 public transport 分别限定两类规划信息，between... 界定路线范围。

sentences.text: There were also links to accommodation in the area.

sentences.text: By registering with the website, users could save their Travel Plan and return to it later, or print it out to take on the visit.

sentences.structure: By doing 表方式或条件；could 后并列 save/return 与 print，to take on the visit 表打印的目的。

sentences.text: The website also had a ‘Your Words’ section where anyone could submit a blog of their New Zealand travels for possible inclusion on the website.
sentences.translation: 网站还设有“你的文字”栏目，任何人都可以提交记录自己新西兰之旅的博客，供网站考虑收录。

sentences.text: The Tourism New Zealand website won two Webby awards for online achievement and innovation.

sentences.text: More importantly perhaps, the growth of tourism to New Zealand was impressive.

vocabulary.meaning: 令人印象深刻的；可观的

sentences.structure: 主干 expenditure increased；by 表增长幅度，per year 表频率，between... 界定统计时段。

sentences.text: From Britain, visits to New Zealand grew at an average annual rate of 13% between 2002 and 2006, compared to a rate of 4% overall for British visits abroad.

sentences.text: The website was set up to allow both individuals and travel organisations to create itineraries and travel packages to suit their own needs and interests.

vocabulary.meaning: 毛利人的会堂及集会场所

sentences.text: Many long-haul travellers enjoy such learning experiences, which provide them with stories to take home to their friends and family.

vocabulary.meaning: 人群中毫不起眼的一员

sentences.translation: 新西兰国土较小，其游客经济主要由小型企业构成。

vocabulary.meaning: 由游客消费带动的经济体系

sentences.text: It is generally perceived as a safe English-speaking country with a reliable transport infrastructure.
sentences.translation: 人们普遍认为，新西兰是一个安全的英语国家，拥有可靠的交通基础设施。
sentences.structure: is perceived as 是正式被动评价结构，不点明评价者；with... 补充构成这种目的地形象的条件。

sentences.text: Because of the long-haul flight, most visitors stay for longer (average 20 days) and want to see as much of the country as possible on what is often seen as a once-in-a-lifetime visit.
sentences.translation: 由于路途遥远，多数游客会停留更久（平均20天），并希望在这趟常被视为一生仅有一次的旅程中，尽可能多地游览这个国家。

vocabulary.meaning: 平均20天；括号中的压缩表达，可展开理解为 an average of 20 days

sentences.text: However, the underlying lessons apply anywhere – the effectiveness of a strong brand, a strategy based on unique experiences and a comprehensive and user-friendly website.
sentences.translation: 然而，这一案例背后的根本启示适用于任何地方——强势品牌的有效性、以独特体验为基础的策略，以及内容全面且方便用户的网站。
sentences.structure: However 扭转“新西兰特殊所以不可复制”的预期；破折号后三项并列解释 underlying lessons，把个案提升为普遍原则。

vocabulary.meaning: 然而；用于转折并把特殊个案提升为普遍结论
背后的根本启示；由案例提炼出的普遍经验
强势品牌；具有清晰定位和影响力的品牌

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 2
readingSections.titleText: Why being bored is stimulating – and useful, too
readingSections.subtitle: This most common of emotions is turning out to be more interesting than we thought

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: We all know how it feels – it’s impossible to keep your mind on anything, time stretches out, and all the things you could do seem equally unlikely to make you feel better. But defining boredom so that it can be studied in the lab has proved difficult. For a start, it can include a lot of other mental states, such as frustration, apathy, depression and indifference. There isn’t even agreement over whether boredom is always a low-energy, flat kind of emotion or whether feeling agitated and restless counts as boredom, too. In his book, Boredom: A Lively History, Peter Toohey at the University of Calgary, Canada, compares it to disgust – an emotion that motivates us to stay away from certain situations. ‘If disgust protects humans from infection, boredom may protect them from “infectious” social situations,’ he suggests.

‘If disgust protects humans from infection, boredom may protect them from “infectious” social situations,’ he suggests.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: By asking people about their experiences of boredom, Thomas Goetz and his team at the University of Konstanz in Germany have recently identified five distinct types: indifferent, calibrating, searching, reactant and apathetic. These can be plotted on two axes – one running left to right, which measures low to high arousal, and the other from top to bottom, which measures how positive or negative the feeling is. Intriguingly, Goetz has found that while people experience all kinds of boredom, they tend to specialise in one. Of the five types, the most damaging is ‘reactant’ boredom with its explosive combination of high arousal and negative emotion. The most useful is what Goetz calls ‘indifferent’ boredom: someone isn’t engaged in anything satisfying but still feels relaxed and calm. However, it remains to be seen whether there are any character traits that predict the kind of boredom each of us might be prone to.

However, it remains to be seen whether there are any character traits that predict the kind of boredom each of us might be prone to.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Psychologist Sandi Mann at the University of Central Lancashire, UK, goes further. ‘All emotions are there for a reason, including boredom,’ she says. Mann has found that being bored makes us more creative. ‘We’re all afraid of being bored but in actual fact it can lead to all kinds of amazing things,’ she says. In experiments published last year, Mann found that people who had been made to feel bored by copying numbers out of the phone book for 15 minutes came up with more creative ideas about how to use a polystyrene cup than a control group. Mann concluded that a passive, boring activity is best for creativity because it allows the mind to wander. In fact, she goes so far as to suggest that we should seek out more boredom in our lives.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Psychologist John Eastwood at York University in Toronto, Canada, isn’t convinced. ‘If you are in a state of mind-wandering you are not bored,’ he says. ‘In my view, by definition boredom is an undesirable state.’ That doesn’t necessarily mean that it isn’t adaptive, he adds. ‘Pain is adaptive – if we didn’t have physical pain, bad things would happen to us. Does that mean that we should actively cause pain? No. But even if boredom has evolved to help us survive, it can still be toxic if allowed to fester.’ For Eastwood, the central feature of boredom is a failure to put our ‘attention system’ into gear. This causes an inability to focus on anything, which makes time seem to go painfully slowly. What’s more, your efforts to improve the situation can end up making you feel worse. ‘People try to connect with the world and if they are not successful there’s that frustration and irritability,’ he says. Perhaps most worryingly, says Eastwood, repeatedly failing to engage attention can lead to a state where we don’t know what to do any more, and no longer care.

Perhaps most worryingly, says Eastwood, repeatedly failing to engage attention can lead to a state where we don’t know what to do any more, and no longer care.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Eastwood’s team is now trying to explore why the attention system fails. It’s early days but they think that at least some of it comes down to personality. Boredom proneness has been linked with a variety of traits. People who are motivated by pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly. Other personality traits, such as curiosity, are associated with a high boredom threshold. More evidence that boredom has detrimental effects comes from studies of people who are more or less prone to boredom. It seems those who bore easily face poorer prospects in education, their career and even life in general. But of course, boredom itself cannot kill — it’s the things we do to deal with it that may put us in danger. What can we do to alleviate it before it comes to that? Goetz’s group has one suggestion. Working with teenagers, they found that those who ‘approach’ a boring situation – in other words, see that it’s boring and get stuck in anyway – report less boredom than those who try to avoid it by using snacks, TV or social media for distraction.

So instead of seeking yet more mental stimulation, perhaps we should leave our phones alone, and use boredom to motivate us to engage with the world in a more meaningful way.

However, it remains to be seen whether there are any character traits that predict the kind of boredom each of us might be prone to.
Psychologist Sandi Mann at the University of Central Lancashire, UK, goes further.
‘All emotions are there for a reason, including boredom,’ she says.
Mann has found that being bored makes us more creative.
‘We’re all afraid of being bored but in actual fact it can lead to all kinds of amazing things,’ she says.

In experiments published last year, Mann found that people who had been made to feel bored by copying numbers out of the phone book for 15 minutes came up with more creative ideas about how to use a polystyrene cup than a control group.
Mann concluded that a passive, boring activity is best for creativity because it allows the mind to wander.
In fact, she goes so far as to suggest that we should seek out more boredom in our lives.
Psychologist John Eastwood at York University in Toronto, Canada, isn’t convinced.
‘If you are in a state of mind-wandering you are not bored,’ he says.
‘In my view, by definition boredom is an undesirable state.’
That doesn’t necessarily mean that it isn’t adaptive, he adds.
‘Pain is adaptive – if we didn’t have physical pain, bad things would happen to us.
Does that mean that we should actively cause pain?
No.
But even if boredom has evolved to help us survive, it can still be toxic if allowed to fester.’
For Eastwood, the central feature of boredom is a failure to put our ‘attention system’ into gear.
This causes an inability to focus on anything, which makes time seem to go painfully slowly.
What’s more, your efforts to improve the situation can end up making you feel worse.
‘People try to connect with the world and if they are not successful there’s that frustration and irritability,’ he says.
Perhaps most worryingly, says Eastwood, repeatedly failing to engage attention can lead to a state where we don’t know what to do any more, and no longer care.
Eastwood’s team is now trying to explore why the attention system fails.
It’s early days but they think that at least some of it comes down to personality.
Boredom proneness has been linked with a variety of traits.
People who are motivated by pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly.
Other personality traits, such as curiosity, are associated with a high boredom threshold.
More evidence that boredom has detrimental effects comes from studies of people who are more or less prone to boredom.
It seems those who bore easily face poorer prospects in education, their career and even life in general.
But of course, boredom itself cannot kill — it’s the things we do to deal with it that may put us in danger.
What can we do to alleviate it before it comes to that?
Goetz’s group has one suggestion.

Working with teenagers, they found that those who ‘approach’ a boring situation – in other words, see that it’s boring and get stuck in anyway – report less boredom than those who try to avoid it by using snacks, TV or social media for distraction.
Psychologist Francoise Wemelsfelder speculates that our over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom.
‘In modern human society there is a lot of overstimulation but still a lot of problems finding meaning,’ she says.
So instead of seeking yet more mental stimulation, perhaps we should leave our phones alone, and use boredom to motivate us to engage with the world in a more meaningful way.

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 3
readingSections.subtitle: Can computers really create works of art?
paragraphs: The Painting Fool is one of a growing number of computer programs which, so their makers claim, possess creative talents. Classical music by an artificial composer has had audiences enraptured, and even tricked them into believing a human was behind the score. Artworks painted by a robot have sold for thousands of dollars and been hung in prestigious galleries. And software has been built which creates art that could not have been imagined by the programmer.

Human beings are the only species to perform sophisticated creative acts regularly. If we can break this process down into computer code, where does that leave human creativity? ‘This is a question at the very core of humanity,’ says Geraint Wiggins, a computational creativity researcher at Goldsmiths, University of London. ‘It scares a lot of people. They are worried that it is taking something special away from what it means to be human.’

To some extent, we are all familiar with computerised art. The question is: where does the work of the artist stop and the creativity of the computer begin? Consider one of the oldest machine artists, Aaron, a robot that has had paintings exhibited in London’s Tate Modern and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Aaron can pick up a paintbrush and paint on canvas on its own. Impressive perhaps, but it is still little more than a tool to realise the programmer’s own creative ideas.

Simon Colton, the designer of the Painting Fool, is keen to make sure his creation doesn’t attract the same criticism. Unlike earlier ‘artists’ such as Aaron, the Painting Fool only needs minimal direction and can come up with its own concepts by going online for material. The software runs its own web searches and trawls through social media sites. It is now beginning to display a kind of imagination too, creating pictures from scratch. One of its original works is a series of fuzzy landscapes, depicting trees and sky. While some might say they have a mechanical look, Colton argues that such reactions arise from people’s double standards towards software-produced and human-produced art. After all, he says, consider that the Painting Fool painted the landscapes without referring to a photo. ‘If a child painted a new scene from its head, you’d say it has a certain level of imagination,’ he points out. ‘The same should be true of a machine.’

Software bugs can also lead to unexpected results. Some of the Painting Fool’s paintings of a chair came out in black and white, thanks to a technical glitch. This gives the work an eerie, ghostlike quality. Human artists like the renowned Ellsworth Kelly are lauded for limiting their colour palette – so why should computers be any different?

Researchers like Colton don’t believe it is right to measure machine creativity directly to that of humans who ‘have had millennia to develop our skills’. Others, though, are fascinated by the prospect that a computer might create something as original and subtle as our best artists. So far, only one has come close. Composer David Cope invented a program called Experiments in Musical Intelligence, or EMI. Not only did EMI create compositions in Cope’s style, but also that of the most revered classical composers, including Bach, Chopin and Mozart. Audiences were moved to tears, and EMI even fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach.

Not everyone was impressed however. Some, such as Wiggins, have blasted Cope’s work as pseudoscience, and condemned him for his deliberately vague explanation of how the software worked. Meanwhile, Douglas Hofstadter of Indiana University said EMI created replicas which still rely completely on the original artist’s creative impulses. When audiences found out the truth they were often outraged with Cope, and one music lover even tried to punch him. Amid such controversy, Cope destroyed EMI’s vital databases.

But why did so many people love the music, yet recoil when they discovered how it was composed? A study by computer scientist David Moffat of Glasgow Caledonian University provides a clue. He asked both expert musicians and non-experts to assess six compositions. The participants weren’t told beforehand whether the tunes were composed by humans or computers, but were asked to guess, and then rate how much they liked each one. People who thought the composer was a computer tended to dislike the piece more than those who believed it was human. This was true even among the experts, who might have been expected to be more objective in their analyses.

Where does this prejudice come from? Paul Bloom of Yale University has a suggestion: he reckons part of the pleasure we get from art stems from the creative process behind the work. This can give it an ‘irresistible essence’, says Bloom. Meanwhile, experiments by Justin Kruger of New York University have shown that people’s enjoyment of an artwork increases if they think more time and effort was needed to create it. Similarly, Colton thinks that when people experience art, they wonder what the artist might have been thinking or what the artist is trying to tell them. It seems obvious, therefore, that with computers producing art, this speculation is cut short – there’s nothing to explore.

But as technology becomes increasingly complex, finding those greater depths in computer art could become possible. This is precisely why Colton asks the Painting Fool to tap into online social networks for its inspiration: hopefully this way it will choose themes that will already be meaningful to us.

questions.prompt: allowed businesses to 1 __________ information regularly

questions.evidence: participating businesses were able to update the details they gave on a regular basis

questions.evidence: the effect of each business on the environment was considered

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.promptZh: F段
questions.evidence: ...our over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom... leave our phones alone, and use boredom to motivate us to engage with the world in a more meaningful way.
questions.explanation: 过度连接是新解释，放下手机并借无聊重新投入世界是新应对，两个部分正对应 iii。

questions.prompt: Peter Toohey
questions.promptZh: 彼得·图希
questions.evidence: If disgust protects humans from infection, boredom may protect them from “infectious” social situations...
questions.explanation: protect...from 与 idea E 的 encourage us to avoid 构成同义改写。

distractorAnalysis.C: 原文无人提出未来下降。

questions.prompt: Thomas Goetz
questions.promptZh: 托马斯·格茨
questions.evidence: Of the five types, the most damaging is ‘reactant’ boredom...
questions.explanation: the most damaging 精确对应 worse than all the others。

questions.prompt: John Eastwood
questions.promptZh: 约翰·伊斯特伍德
questions.evidence: What’s more, your efforts to improve the situation can end up making you feel worse.
questions.explanation: efforts to improve 对应 trying to cope，feel worse 对应 increase negative effects。

questions.prompt: Francoise Wemelsfelder
questions.promptZh: 弗朗索瓦丝·韦梅尔斯费尔德
questions.evidence: ...our over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom.
questions.explanation: over-connected lifestyles 与 the way we live today 同义，new source 对应 encourage boredom。

questions.prompt: people cannot 24 ______, due to a failure in what he calls the ‘attention system’
questions.promptZh: 由于所谓“注意力系统”失灵，人们无法______
questions.evidence: This causes an inability to focus on anything...
questions.explanation: cannot 后接动词原形；原文 inability to focus 直接改写为 cannot focus。ONE WORD ONLY，不能写 focus on。

distractorAnalysis.engage: 后文是 engage attention，不直接对应 cannot 后的中心能力表述。
distractorAnalysis.attention: 词性不合，cannot 后需动词。
distractorAnalysis.concentrate: 语义可通但不是原文词。

questions.prompt: those for whom 25 ______ is an important aim in life may have problems in coping with boredom
questions.promptZh: 把______视为人生重要目标的人可能难以应对无聊
questions.evidence: People who are motivated by pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly.
questions.explanation: motivated by pleasure 被改写为 pleasure is an important aim；空格需名词，答案为原文单词 pleasure。

distractorAnalysis.personality: 范围过大，原文明确指出具体动机。
distractorAnalysis.motivation: 不是原文对应目标的词。
distractorAnalysis.satisfaction: 虽语义相关，但不是证据句用词。

questions.prompt: those who have the characteristic of 26 ______ can generally cope with it
questions.promptZh: 具有______这一特质的人通常能应对无聊
questions.evidence: Other personality traits, such as curiosity, are associated with a high boredom threshold.
questions.explanation: high boredom threshold 表示较能承受无聊；characteristic of 后接名词，原文为 curiosity。

distractorAnalysis.threshold: 它是结果指标，不是人的特质内容。
distractorAnalysis.curious: 词性不合，of 后此处需要名词且必须取原文一词。

questions.prompt: What is the writer suggesting about computer-produced works in the first paragraph?
questions.promptZh: 作者在第一段对计算机创作的作品作出了什么暗示？

options.A: People’s acceptance of them can vary considerably.
options.B: A great deal of progress has already been attained in this field.
options.C: They have had more success in some artistic genres than in others.
options.D: The advances are not as significant as the public believes them to be.

questions.evidence: Classical music by an artificial composer has had audiences enraptured ... Artworks painted by a robot have sold for thousands of dollars ... And software has been built which creates art that could not have been imagined by the programmer.
questions.explanation: 三个并列实例分别说明机器音乐能打动并欺骗听众、机器人画作进入名贵画廊、软件甚至能产生程序员未预想到的艺术，合起来强调该领域已取得大量进展。

distractorAnalysis.A: 段中列举不同成果，不是在比较公众接受度的波动。
distractorAnalysis.C: 没有比较不同艺术门类谁更成功。
distractorAnalysis.D: 作者强调成果显著，并未说公众高估进步。

questions.prompt: According to Geraint Wiggins, why are many people worried by computer art?
questions.promptZh: 根据 Geraint Wiggins 的说法，为什么许多人担忧计算机艺术？

options.A: It is aesthetically inferior to human art.
options.B: It may ultimately supersede human art.
options.C: It undermines a fundamental human quality.
options.D: It will lead to a deterioration in human ability.

questions.evidence: They are worried that it is taking something special away from what it means to be human.
questions.explanation: “从身为人类的意义中拿走某种特殊之物”对应“削弱一种根本的人类特质”。

distractorAnalysis.A: Wiggins 没有评价机器艺术审美低劣。
distractorAnalysis.B: 没有说机器艺术最终会取代人类艺术。
distractorAnalysis.D: 担忧指向人类独特性的定义，而非人的能力退化。

questions.prompt: What is a key difference between Aaron and the Painting Fool?
questions.promptZh: Aaron 与 Painting Fool 的关键区别是什么？

options.C: the source of its subject matter
options.D: the technical standard of its output

questions.evidence: Aaron ... is still little more than a tool to realise the programmer’s own creative ideas. Unlike earlier ‘artists’ such as Aaron, the Painting Fool only needs minimal direction and can come up with its own concepts by going online for material.
questions.explanation: Aaron 的题材与创意来自程序员；Painting Fool 会联网取材并形成自己的概念，差异在题材来源。

distractorAnalysis.A: 文中没有比较两位程序员的背景。
distractorAnalysis.B: 未把公众反应作为两者差别。
distractorAnalysis.D: 没有比较输出的技术水准。

questions.prompt: What point does Simon Colton make in the fourth paragraph?
questions.promptZh: Simon Colton 在第四段提出了什么观点？

options.A: Software-produced art is often dismissed as childish and simplistic.
options.B: The same concepts of creativity should not be applied to all forms of art.
options.C: It is unreasonable to expect a machine to be as imaginative as a human being.
options.D: People tend to judge computer art and human art according to different criteria.

questions.evidence: Colton argues that such reactions arise from people’s double standards towards software-produced and human-produced art. ... ‘The same should be true of a machine.’
questions.explanation: 核心词是 double standards：人们用不同标准判断机器艺术与人类艺术。

distractorAnalysis.A: 文中只说有些人觉得画面机械，并非幼稚简单。
distractorAnalysis.B: Colton 主张同一想象力标准也应适用于机器，恰与本项相反。
distractorAnalysis.C: 他没有降低对机器想象力的期待，而是在要求公平判断。

questions.prompt: The writer refers to the paintings of a chair as an example of computer art which
questions.promptZh: 作者提及椅子画，是把它作为哪一类计算机艺术的例子？

options.B: exhibits a certain level of genuine artistic skill.
options.C: closely resembles that of a well-known artist.
options.D: highlights the technical limitations of the software.

questions.evidence: Some of the Painting Fool’s paintings of a chair came out in black and white, thanks to a technical glitch. This gives the work an eerie, ghostlike quality.
questions.explanation: 技术故障意外带来“诡异、幽灵般”的鲜明效果，因此选 A。

distractorAnalysis.B: 作者描述效果，没有据此认定真正艺术技巧。
distractorAnalysis.C: Ellsworth Kelly 只是被用来作公平标准的类比，不是说画作与他相似。
distractorAnalysis.D: 故障是成因，但段落强调它产生的艺术效果，而非软件局限。

questions.prompt: Simon Colton says it is important to consider the long-term view when
questions.promptZh: Simon Colton 说，在何种情况下应当采取长远眼光？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: Researchers like Colton don’t believe it is right to measure machine creativity directly to that of humans who ‘have had millennia to develop our skills’.
questions.explanation: “人类已有数千年发展技能”要求在比较人机艺术成就时采用长期尺度，故 D。

distractorAnalysis.A: 这是 EMI 的惊人表现，对应第 33 题。
distractorAnalysis.B: 这是 Moffat 实验的盲测条件，对应第 37 题。
distractorAnalysis.C: 这是 Hofstadter 对 EMI 的批评，对应第 35 题。
distractorAnalysis.E: 这是 Wiggins 指责 Cope 未做之事，对应第 34 题。
distractorAnalysis.F: 文中没有说 Colton 的长远观点用于说服公众。
distractorAnalysis.G: 这是听众愤怒的触发因素，对应第 36 题。

questions.prompt: David Cope’s EMI software surprised people by
questions.promptZh: David Cope 的 EMI 软件以何种表现令人大吃一惊？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: EMI even fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach.
questions.explanation: 连古典音乐专家都误以为是真正的巴赫，说明作品与人类作品几乎无法区分，故 A。

distractorAnalysis.B: EMI 不是判断作者身份的主体。
distractorAnalysis.C: 这是批评而非令人惊讶的成就。
distractorAnalysis.D: EMI 没有进行人机成就比较。
distractorAnalysis.E: Cope 恰被批评没有披露技术细节。
distractorAnalysis.F: 没有说软件主动劝服公众。
distractorAnalysis.G: 发现机器身份的是听众，对应第 36 题。

questions.prompt: Geraint Wiggins criticised Cope for not
questions.promptZh: Geraint Wiggins 批评 Cope 没有做什么？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: Wiggins ... condemned him for his deliberately vague explanation of how the software worked.
questions.explanation: “故意含糊地解释软件原理”就是没有公开程序的技术细节，故 E。

distractorAnalysis.A: Wiggins 的批评不是作品不像人类。
distractorAnalysis.B: 与 Cope 是否知道创作者身份无关。
distractorAnalysis.D: 没有要求 Cope 比较人机成就。
distractorAnalysis.F: 没有批评他未劝服公众。
distractorAnalysis.G: 不是要求 Cope 发现作品来源。

questions.prompt: Douglas Hofstadter claimed that EMI was
questions.promptZh: Douglas Hofstadter 声称 EMI 是怎样的？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: EMI created replicas which still rely completely on the original artist’s creative impulses.
questions.explanation: replicas 且 completely rely on 原艺术家的创意冲动，等于作品完全依赖其创作者的想象力，故 C。

distractorAnalysis.A: 这是 EMI 欺骗专家所显示的表面相似度，不是 Hofstadter 的批评重点。
distractorAnalysis.B: 不是 EMI 在辨认作品来源。
distractorAnalysis.D: 他没有说 EMI 比较成就。
distractorAnalysis.G: 发现机器来源的是听众。

questions.prompt: Audiences who had listened to EMI’s music became angry after
questions.promptZh: 听过 EMI 音乐的听众在发生什么之后变得愤怒？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: When audiences found out the truth they were often outraged with Cope.
questions.explanation: truth 指音乐由程序生成；得知这一来源后听众才愤怒，故 G。

distractorAnalysis.A: 作品像人类作品原本让人感动，并非生气的时间触发点。
distractorAnalysis.B: 不是“知道是否”，而是明确发现来自软件。
distractorAnalysis.C: 听众并非因依赖创作者想象力而怒。

questions.prompt: The participants in David Moffat’s study had to assess music without
questions.promptZh: David Moffat 研究中的参与者必须在不知道什么的情况下评价音乐？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: The participants weren’t told beforehand whether the tunes were composed by humans or computers, but were asked to guess, and then rate how much they liked each one.
questions.explanation: 参与者事先不知道曲子由人还是计算机创作，故 B。

distractorAnalysis.A: 不是参与者自己生成作品。
distractorAnalysis.C: 不是评价前被隐瞒的具体信息。
distractorAnalysis.D: 他们评价曲目，不是直接比较人机历史成就。
distractorAnalysis.E: 与 Cope 程序细节无关。
distractorAnalysis.F: 参与者没有承担劝服公众的任务。
distractorAnalysis.G: G 表示已经发现是程序产品，与“without knowing”相反。

questions.prompt: Moffat’s research may help explain people’s reactions to EMI.
questions.promptZh: Moffat 的研究或许有助于解释人们对 EMI 的反应。

options.NOT GIVEN: the writer’s view is impossible to determine

questions.evidence: But why did so many people love the music, yet recoil when they discovered how it was composed? A study by computer scientist David Moffat ... provides a clue.
questions.explanation: 作者先提出听众得知来源后反感之谜，紧接着说 Moffat 的研究“provides a clue”，明确支持题干。

distractorAnalysis.NO: 原文不是否认解释力，而是说研究提供线索。
distractorAnalysis.NOT GIVEN: 作者已明确表达研究与反应之间的解释关系。

questions.prompt: The non-experts in Moffat’s study all responded in a predictable way.
questions.promptZh: Moffat 研究中的非专家全都以一种可预测的方式作出了反应。

options.NOT GIVEN: the writer’s view is impossible to determine

questions.evidence: People who thought the composer was a computer tended to dislike the piece more ... This was true even among the experts.
questions.explanation: 原文只给总体倾向，并说专家中也有这一倾向；没有说明非专家是否“全都”如此，也没有评价其反应是否可预测。

distractorAnalysis.YES: tended to 不能推出 all，也没有 predictable。
distractorAnalysis.NO: 原文同样没有明确说非专家并非全部如此，因此不能判 NO。

questions.prompt: Justin Kruger’s findings cast doubt on Paul Bloom’s theory about people’s prejudice towards computer art.
questions.promptZh: Justin Kruger 的研究结果使 Paul Bloom 关于人们对计算机艺术偏见的理论受到质疑。

options.NOT GIVEN: the writer’s view is impossible to determine

questions.evidence: he reckons part of the pleasure we get from art stems from the creative process behind the work. ... experiments by Justin Kruger ... have shown that people’s enjoyment of an artwork increases if they think more time and effort was needed to create it.
questions.explanation: Kruger 发现人们认为创作投入越多便越享受作品，正好支持 Bloom 所说愉悦部分源于创作过程，因此题干“cast doubt”与原文相反。

distractorAnalysis.YES: 两项观点是相互支持，不是质疑。
distractorAnalysis.NOT GIVEN: 原文并列呈现两者，并清楚显示逻辑一致，足以判断为 NO。
